unit_name: Conflict and Tension in the Gulf and Afghanistan, 1990-2009

lessons.title: Regional Instability After the Iran-Iraq War
lessons.description: How an eight-year war left Iraq armed, indebted and looking outward for someone to blame.
spec_bullets_covered: Regional instability — consequences of Iran-Iraq war
key_content: 1980-88 war: scale, casualties, chemical weapons, stalemate ending
Saddam emerges with $80bn debt ($35bn external, ~$15bn to Kuwait) and a million-man army
Iraqi economy crippled by collapsed oil price; reconstruction needs unmet
Saddam's claim of having defended the Arab world against Iranian revolution
Cult of personality and Ba'athist regime tightening grip on Iraqi society
lessons.exam_focus: Narrative — write an account of how the Iran-Iraq war created tensions in the Gulf
lessons.misconception_addressed: That the Iran-Iraq war ended cleanly in 1988; in fact unresolved debts and grievances directly fed the 1990 invasion

lessons.title: Western, Russian and Regional Interests in the Gulf
lessons.description: Why outside powers cared so much about a strip of sand and the oil beneath it.
spec_bullets_covered: Western and Russian interests in and attitudes towards Iran and Iraq
Threat to oil supplies
Israeli-Palestinian conflict's contribution to Gulf tension and motives for global terrorism
key_content: Cold War legacy: USSR's earlier ties to Iraq vs USA's ties to Iran's Shah, then post-1979 reset
Western dependence on Gulf oil; choke point at Strait of Hormuz
USA tilting towards Iraq during Iran-Iraq war to contain Iran
Israeli-Palestinian conflict: First Intifada 1987-93, perception of US bias as a recruitment tool for jihadists
Saudi Arabia, Egypt and the wider Arab order as US allies hosting Western forces
lessons.exam_focus: Source utility — how useful are sources for understanding why the Gulf mattered to outside powers
lessons.misconception_addressed: That Cold War rivalry ended in 1991 and stopped shaping the region; in practice old alignments and interests persisted

lessons.title: The Invasion of Kuwait, August 1990
lessons.description: Saddam gambles that a fait accompli will solve his debts and silence his rivals.
spec_bullets_covered: Reasons for the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
key_content: Iraq's grievances: oil overproduction by Kuwait, alleged slant-drilling at the Rumaila field
Failed Jeddah negotiations, July 1990
Saddam's meeting with US Ambassador April Glaspie — perception of an American green light
Invasion plan changes from limited grab to full annexation; Kuwait declared 19th province
Iraqi forces overrun Kuwait City in hours; al-Sabah ruling family flees to Saudi Arabia
lessons.exam_focus: Source analysis — what does a source suggest about Saddam's motives for invading Kuwait
lessons.misconception_addressed: That Saddam's motives were purely ideological; the trigger was an economic crisis with concrete cash and oil grievances

lessons.title: Bush, Thatcher and Building the Coalition
lessons.description: How a horrified White House and a steely Downing Street turned outrage into a 35-nation army.
spec_bullets_covered: Reactions and roles of Bush and Thatcher
The UN campaign against Saddam Hussein
key_content: Thatcher's Aspen meeting with Bush, 'don't go wobbly' line
UN Security Council Resolution 660 demanding withdrawal; Resolution 678 setting 15 January 1991 ultimatum
Operation Desert Shield: deployment to Saudi Arabia at King Fahd's invitation
Coalition of 35 nations including Egypt, Syria, Saudi Arabia — Arab cover crucial to US strategy
Funding by Saudi Arabia, Kuwait-in-exile, Germany and Japan; British Operation Granby
lessons.exam_focus: Narrative — write an account of how the international community responded to the invasion of Kuwait
lessons.misconception_addressed: That the coalition was purely Western; without Arab and Soviet diplomatic backing the campaign would not have launched

lessons.title: Operation Desert Storm and the End of the 1991 War
lessons.description: Five weeks of bombing, one hundred hours of ground war, and a ceasefire that solved little.
spec_bullets_covered: Consequences of the war
US influence in the region
Arab reactions
key_content: Air campaign 17 January — 23 February: 100,000 sorties, precision-guided weapons debut
Iraqi Scud missile attacks on Israel and Saudi Arabia; Patriot defence
Ground campaign 24-28 February: 100-hour rout, 'Highway of Death' on Basra road
Bush's decision not to march on Baghdad; ceasefire 28 February, 392 coalition dead
Failed Shia and Kurdish uprisings spring 1991; Saddam survives, no-fly zones imposed
Arab world divided — Jordan, PLO and Yemen sided with Iraq, exposing fault lines
lessons.exam_focus: Source essay — how far do sources show that Operation Desert Storm achieved its aims
lessons.misconception_addressed: That the 1991 war ended Saddam's regime; he stayed in power for another twelve years and crushed internal revolts

lessons.title: Al-Qaeda: Aims, Beliefs and Bin Laden
lessons.description: How a Saudi millionaire turned Cold War mujahideen into a global jihadist franchise.
spec_bullets_covered: Aims of Al-Qaeda and the role of Osama bin Laden
key_content: Soviet-Afghan war 1979-89 as the 'crucible' — Arab Afghan volunteers, Maktab al-Khidamat
Bin Laden's background: Saudi wealthy family, religious radicalisation, work with Abdullah Azzam
Founding of al-Qaeda ('the base'), Peshawar, 1988
Anger at US troops on Saudi soil after 1991 — 'crusader-Zionist alliance' rhetoric
1996 and 1998 fatwas declaring war on Americans; 1998 US embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania
2000 USS Cole bombing; growing intelligence warnings
lessons.exam_focus: Narrative — write an account of how al-Qaeda developed between 1988 and 2001
lessons.misconception_addressed: That al-Qaeda began with 9/11; it had been operating, bombing and recruiting for over a decade beforehand

lessons.title: 11 September 2001: The Attacks That Changed the World
lessons.description: A single morning in New York and Washington that triggered two wars and a generation of change.
spec_bullets_covered: 11 September attacks
key_content: Hijackers, planning, training in Afghan camps; lead role of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
The four flights: World Trade Center North and South, Pentagon, Flight 93 (Shanksville)
Casualties: 2,977 killed; collapse of the Twin Towers broadcast live
Immediate global response — NATO invokes Article 5 for the first time
Bush's address to Congress 20 September — 'either you are with us, or with the terrorists'
Long-term cultural impact: surveillance state, airport security, Islamophobia
lessons.exam_focus: Source utility — how useful are sources for understanding the impact of the 9/11 attacks
lessons.misconception_addressed: That 9/11 was simply a Middle Eastern attack; the planners trained worldwide and the response was a global geopolitical shift

lessons.title: The Taliban and Afghanistan as a Rogue State
lessons.description: How a movement of religious students seized a country and gave al-Qaeda a sanctuary.
spec_bullets_covered: Afghanistan: its reputation as a rogue state
The Taliban regime
Western and Muslim attitudes to its policies
Problems faced by ethnic groups
key_content: Post-Soviet civil war 1992-96: warlord rule, Najibullah's fall
Origins of the Taliban: Pashtun madrasa students in Pakistan, led by Mullah Omar
Capture of Kabul 1996; treatment of women — banned from work, education, public life
Treatment of ethnic minorities (Hazara, Tajik, Uzbek), 1998 Mazar-i-Sharif massacre
Destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas, March 2001 — international outcry
Sheltering bin Laden; Western and most Muslim states refusing recognition (only Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, UAE recognised)
lessons.exam_focus: Source analysis — what does a source suggest about the Taliban regime
lessons.misconception_addressed: That all Muslims supported the Taliban; in practice most Muslim-majority states refused recognition and condemned its excesses

lessons.title: Bush's War on Terror and Operation Enduring Freedom
lessons.description: Bush demands the Taliban hand over bin Laden; the Taliban refuse, and the bombs fall.
spec_bullets_covered: Bush's war against terror — Bush's aims
Blair's support for intervention — the 2001 US/UK operation
Overthrow of the Taliban and collapse of its regime
key_content: Bush's 'war on terror' doctrine: pre-emption, unilateralism if necessary, 'axis of evil' framing
Blair's 'shoulder to shoulder' speech, 11 September 2001
Taliban refuses to hand over bin Laden without proof
Operation Enduring Freedom launches 7 October 2001: US/UK air campaign, CIA Special Activities, Northern Alliance ground troops
Fall of Mazar-i-Sharif, Kabul (13 November), Kandahar (December); battle of Tora Bora — bin Laden escapes
Speed of Taliban collapse caused by ground proxies and air power, not large Western forces
lessons.exam_focus: Narrative — write an account of how the Taliban regime was overthrown in 2001
lessons.misconception_addressed: That the West conquered Afghanistan with massed troops; in 2001 victory was won mostly by Afghan proxy forces backed by airstrikes

lessons.title: Karzai, Bonn and the Long Resurgence of the Taliban
lessons.description: A new Kabul government, a UN promise, and the warlords who never went away.
spec_bullets_covered: UN peace conference
Problems faced by Karzai's government
Resurgence of the Taliban
key_content: December 2001 Bonn Conference: agreement excluding the Taliban; Karzai becomes interim leader
ISAF deployment under UN mandate; light Western footprint outside Kabul
Karzai's reliance on regional warlords; corruption, weak central government
Loya Jirga 2002, new constitution 2004, presidential elections 2004
Taliban regroups in Pakistan tribal areas 2002-05; insurgency spreads to south and east
NATO takes lead 2006; British forces in Helmand from 2006; opium economy fuels insurgency
lessons.exam_focus: Source utility — how useful are sources for understanding the problems faced by Karzai's government
lessons.misconception_addressed: That the 2001 victory was permanent; by 2006 the Taliban had regrouped and the war became a far longer counter-insurgency

lessons.title: Saddam, WMD and the Road to the 2003 Invasion
lessons.description: Inspectors, intelligence dossiers and a White House that had decided long before.
spec_bullets_covered: Saddam Hussein's regime — treatment of Kurds and Shia Muslims
Debate about Iraq's links to Al-Qaeda and its reputation as a rogue state
Religious divisions in Iraq
International attitudes towards Saddam Hussein and the role of the UN
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors and the issue of Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD)
key_content: Saddam's record: 1988 Halabja gas attack on Kurds, 1991 Shia uprising massacres, marsh Arabs
1990s sanctions, oil-for-food, no-fly zones, low-level air strikes
Bush administration's claim of Saddam-al-Qaeda links — later refuted by 9/11 Commission
UN Resolution 1441, November 2002 — final opportunity to comply
IAEA (Hans Blix, ElBaradei) finding no clear evidence of active WMD programmes
UK 'September Dossier' 2002, 'forty-five minute' claim; February 2003 anti-war protests, biggest in UK history
Failure to secure second UN resolution; coalition assembled outside UN authorisation
lessons.exam_focus: Source essay — how far do sources support the view that the 2003 invasion of Iraq was justified
lessons.misconception_addressed: That intelligence was clear-cut on WMD; both Hutton (2004) and Chilcot (2016) showed it was contested and selectively presented

lessons.title: Invasion, Insurgency and Iraq by 2009
lessons.description: From the fall of Baghdad to the surge — eight years that ended with a country still in pieces.
spec_bullets_covered: The military campaign
Western interests, including oil
Opposition to the invasion within Iraq and internationally
Downfall of Saddam Hussein
Impact of war on the Iraqi people and across the world
The Insurgency
Elections and transfer of powers to National Assembly
Global anti-US and anti-UK terrorism
2007 US troop surge
Stability of Iraq by the end of Bush's Presidency
key_content: Invasion launched 20 March 2003; Baghdad falls 9 April; statue of Saddam pulled down
Bush's 'Mission Accomplished' speech, 1 May 2003 — premature
CPA decisions: de-Ba'athification and disbanding the Iraqi army create unemployed armed Sunni population
Insurgency 2003-06: IEDs, foreign jihadists, Sunni-Shia civil war 2006-07
Abu Ghraib abuse photos 2004; loss of moral authority
Saddam captured December 2003, executed December 2006
Madrid bombings 2004, London 7/7 bombings 2005 as global blowback
January 2005 Iraqi elections; Maliki government
2007 surge under Petraeus and Sunni 'Awakening' reduce violence
Status of Forces Agreement: US combat troops out by December 2011; Iraq fragile but standing by January 2009
lessons.exam_focus: Source essay — how far do sources show that Iraq was stable by the end of Bush's presidency
lessons.misconception_addressed: That the war ended when Baghdad fell in 2003; the deadliest years were 2005-07, and the country was not stable by 2009

teaching_brief.unit_overview: AQA's newest and least-taught wider world depth study, sometimes nicknamed 'the Saddam option'. Three contained chunks: the 1990-91 Gulf War (4 lessons), 9/11 and Afghanistan (3 lessons), the Iraq War 2003-09 (5 lessons). Lessons 1-2 set up regional tensions; lessons 3-5 cover the first war; lessons 6-10 swing the focus to al-Qaeda, 9/11 and Afghanistan; lessons 11-12 close with Iraq 2003-09. Recent history with strong primary-source material (TV news, photographs, official inquiries) suits the source-heavy paper.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the 2003 Iraq invasion was a direct response to 9/11 and that Saddam was operationally linked to al-Qaeda.
common_misconceptions.correction: The 9/11 Commission Report (2004) and the Senate Intelligence Committee found no operational link. Saddam's secular Ba'athist regime and bin Laden's Sunni jihadism were ideologically opposed. The link was a post-hoc justification, not a cause.
common_misconceptions.source: 9/11 Commission Report (2004); RUSI commentary on Iraq Inquiry

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think the 1991 Gulf War ended Saddam's regime.
common_misconceptions.correction: Bush deliberately stopped short of Baghdad. Saddam crushed Shia and Kurdish uprisings in spring 1991 and stayed in power until April 2003 — twelve more years of sanctions, no-fly zones and continued repression.
common_misconceptions.source: Imperial War Museum, Operation Desert Storm: The Aftermath of the Gulf War

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students believe the Afghanistan war began in 2001.
common_misconceptions.correction: Afghanistan had been at war almost continuously since the 1979 Soviet invasion. The Soviet-Afghan war (1979-89), the civil war of warlords (1992-96), and the Taliban takeover (1996) all preceded Operation Enduring Freedom. Al-Qaeda itself was a direct legacy of the anti-Soviet jihad.
common_misconceptions.source: RUSI 9/11 Reading List: Al-Qa'ida before the Twin Towers; History Today, 'Before the Taliban'

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the WMD intelligence was either obviously correct or a deliberate lie.
common_misconceptions.correction: The Hutton Report (2004) and Chilcot Report (2016) both showed the intelligence was contested. Chilcot found that No. 10 took 'the most optimistic top line of every issue and played down the problems and the caveats and the warnings'. The failing was hubris and selective presentation, not fraud.
common_misconceptions.source: Iraq Inquiry (Chilcot Report) 2016, RUSI 'Chilcot — The Judgement of History', IISS analysis

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think the Iraq War ended in 2003 when Baghdad fell.
common_misconceptions.correction: The fall of Baghdad began the war's bloodiest phase. The 2003-06 insurgency, 2006-07 sectarian civil war, the 2007 surge and the gradual transition to Iraqi forces meant US combat troops did not formally leave until December 2011. By 2009 Iraq was fragile but no longer in open civil war.
common_misconceptions.source: RUSI 'Iraq War — Ten Years On'; IISS 'An Iraq Syndrome?'

examiner_signals.signal: This option's source pool is recent enough that students often have personal/family memory of events. Examiners reward those who place sources in their proper political context (e.g. a 2002 dossier vs a 2016 inquiry) rather than treating recency as automatic reliability.
examiner_signals.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 1 Section B source-utility questions

examiner_signals.signal: Narrative-account questions on this option often ask about a single short period (e.g. 'events of August 1990' or 'the 2001 campaign in Afghanistan'). Examiners want a chain of cause-and-consequence, not a list of dates.
examiner_signals.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 1 Section B narrative-account questions

examiner_signals.signal: 16-mark source-based essays must reach a substantiated overall judgement. On this option judgements typically weigh military success against political failure (1991 ceasefire) or short-term overthrow against long-term insurgency (2003-09).
examiner_signals.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.1 and principal examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section B

examiner_signals.signal: Specialist vocabulary required: insurgency, coalition, sanctions, regime change, jihad, sectarian, pre-emption, no-fly zone, fatwa. Avoiding this register caps SPaG marks at the threshold band.
examiner_signals.source: AQA spec section 4.4.3 SPaG performance descriptors

pedagogical_notes.note: Front-load the second-order concept of 'tension' — students need to distinguish economic tension (oil, debt, sanctions), ideological tension (jihadism vs secular regimes vs Western liberalism), and ethnic/sectarian tension (Sunni-Shia, Pashtun-Tajik) so they can deploy them in extended responses.
pedagogical_notes.source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools (disciplinary vocabulary)

pedagogical_notes.note: Source/interpretation work on this option benefits from teacher modelling because students lack period instinct. Walk through how to read a 2002 newspaper editorial vs a 2016 retrospective vs a personal memoir.
Comparative judgement (1991 vs 2003 wars; Afghanistan vs Iraq insurgencies) is consistently the hardest skill at GCSE — schedule explicit retrieval and worked examples on the 16-mark question type.
pedagogical_notes.source: Cambridge Assessment Network and Research, history specifications

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Saddam Hussein
key_individuals_and_groups.role: President of Iraq 1979-2003; invaded Kuwait 1990, deposed and executed after 2003 Iraq War

key_individuals_and_groups.name: George H. W. Bush
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US President 1989-93; built the 1991 coalition and ordered Operation Desert Storm

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Margaret Thatcher
key_individuals_and_groups.role: UK Prime Minister 1979-90; backed Bush at Aspen and committed UK forces (Operation Granby)

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Norman Schwarzkopf
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Commander of the US-led coalition during Operation Desert Storm

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Osama bin Laden
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda; planned the 1998 embassy bombings, USS Cole, and 9/11 attacks

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mullah Omar
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Founder and leader of the Taliban; ruled Afghanistan as Emir 1996-2001

key_individuals_and_groups.name: George W. Bush
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US President 2001-09; declared the war on terror, ordered the 2001 Afghanistan and 2003 Iraq invasions

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Tony Blair
key_individuals_and_groups.role: UK Prime Minister 1997-2007; backed both invasions; subject of the Hutton and Chilcot inquiries

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hamid Karzai
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Interim then elected President of Afghanistan 2001-14; chosen at Bonn 2001

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hans Blix
key_individuals_and_groups.role: UN/UNMOVIC chief weapons inspector; reported limited evidence of active WMD programmes pre-2003

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mohamed ElBaradei
key_individuals_and_groups.role: IAEA Director General; said Iraq's nuclear documents looked forged

key_individuals_and_groups.name: David Petraeus
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US general; commanded the 2007 surge in Iraq, later CENTCOM commander

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Al-Qaeda
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Sunni jihadist network founded 1988 in Peshawar; carried out 9/11 attacks

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Taliban
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Pashtun Islamist movement; ruled most of Afghanistan 1996-2001 and led post-2001 insurgency

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Northern Alliance
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Tajik/Uzbek-led anti-Taliban coalition; US ground proxy in 2001

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Paul Bremer's US-led occupation administration in Iraq 2003-04; ordered de-Ba'athification
